scenes.title: Whose voice comes first?
scenes.speaker: scribe
text: The bus horn is the last sound you remember. You pushed a stranger out of its path. A flash of white. Then heat, mudbrick, and a hand shaking your shoulder.

Your hands are older. Your clothes are linen. Somehow the words around you make sense. ‘Administrator? They have been waiting since dawn.’ Djehu presses a seal into your palm. Outside, a line of people bends around the grain store. The seal gives you authority: a recognized right to decide. It does not prove your decisions will be just.

You are responsible for this estate’s village. The river rose poorly; a canal bank has collapsed. Your store holds 60 measures of food grain and 20 of seed grain. These are simplified game units, not a reconstruction of ancient accounting. You cannot buy your way out with money you do not have.
Under the seal lies a smooth dark stone. A pale line flickers inside it. Djehu does not seem to notice. ‘The landholder expects to be heard first,’ he says. Behind him, a woman holds an empty basket.
scenes.asideTitle: Ask Djehu what the seal means
scenes.aside: ‘It makes your orders official. It does not make them wise.’ He taps his board. ‘My duty is to record what leaves this store. Yours is harder: deciding whose needs the record should notice. If you make me hide the shortage, I can keep a tidy account of a dying village.’ You remember a question from your old classroom: who gets to decide what is right? Here, unsettlingly, the answer is you.
choices: listen
Hear the households and workers before making promises.
ledger
Inspect the stores and ask who is missing from the account.
command
Receive the landholder first; authority needs influential friends.

responses.listen: Tia steps forward. Hori leaves the back of the queue. Djehu adds two names to the hearing. You have not fed anyone yet, but people who expected silence now expect an answer.
responses.ledger: The account lists sacks, not mouths. You ask for the households it does not include. Djehu pauses, then opens a second tablet. Your question has changed what counts as evidence.
responses.command: Intef enters. The queue falls quiet. That silence feels efficient until you notice Tia turning her basket upside down, so everyone can see that it is empty.

scenes.title: The first bread
scenes.speaker: household
text: ‘My neighbor has three children,’ Tia says. ‘My brother has two strong sons who can work. If you give each house the same amount, it will look fair on the board. It will not last the same number of days.’ Djehu says equal shares are the custom—the established way of doing things. Tia asks whether a familiar rule still fits this year’s needs.

Djehu suggests a public feast: it would restore confidence. Hori wants food held for the people repairing the canal. Tia notices your own untouched breakfast. ‘You should eat too. But please do not make my children wait until you understand everything.’

A needs-based ration costs 16 measures. Equal household shares cost 18. A feast costs 36. There is no outside delivery you can simply assume will arrive. Your first order will teach the village what kind of fairness to expect.
scenes.asideTitle: Ask Tia about people who cannot queue
scenes.aside: ‘A widow on the east lane cannot walk here. Two families work fields beyond the canal. They never heard there would be a hearing. Let us carry their shares, and let someone check that we did.’ Considering everyone requires more than listening to whoever is loudest or nearest. Her request has reasons behind it: different needs and barriers to access, not simply a wish for special treatment.
choices: needs
Distribute by need, with public reasons and delivery to absent households (16 grain).
equal
Give every household an equal share (18 grain).
feast
Hold a generous feast to end today’s hunger and fear (36 grain).
reserve
Keep the store closed until the influential families agree.

responses.needs: The amounts differ, so you explain the reasons aloud. Tia agrees to deliver the absent households’ shares with a witness. Some people grumble. They can at least question the rule.
responses.equal: The line moves quickly. Tia accepts her share, then quietly gives some to a larger household. Your equal rule has left neighbors to repair its unequal effects.
responses.feast: For a few hours, the courtyard is full of laughter. You remember that relief matters. When the pots are empty, Djehu shows you the remaining grain. Tomorrow will still arrive.
responses.reserve: The doors remain shut. Your order preserves every measure of grain and spends something less visible: people’s belief that waiting patiently will help them.

scenes.title: Who repairs the water?
scenes.speaker: worker
text: Hori spreads reeds across the ground to show the broken canal. ‘Repair the bank properly and the next water will reach the lower fields. Patch the top and it will look sound from the road. Until it breaks.’
The workers need rations. They also have families and fields of their own. Intef says you can require service. Hori replies, ‘You can command our hands. Hunger will still decide how long they work.’

A paid crew costs 12 grain. A shorter shared-work schedule costs 6 and requires some of your own time. Forced labor saves grain but places the burden on people with little power to refuse. Delaying leaves the lower fields exposed. These are consequences: what your decision makes happen, including costs that appear after the applause.
scenes.asideTitle: Ask Hori why he doubts the quick repair
scenes.aside: ‘My father patched this bank twice. Each time the water cut underneath it. We need to strengthen the base.’ He is not asking you to ignore the account. He is asking you to count knowledge that never appears on it.
choices: paid
Pay a crew and use Hori’s deeper repair plan (12 grain).
shared
Agree on shorter shifts and share the work yourself (6 grain).
forced
Require unpaid work; the canal serves everyone.
delay
Delay repairs and preserve today’s supplies.

responses.paid: Hori marks the base of the bank, not just its visible edge. The crew receives food before work. You have fewer reserves and a repair people have a reason to maintain.
responses.shared: The schedule leaves workers time for their own fields. Your back aches by midday. Hori warns you that shared effort works only if tomorrow’s administrator respects the agreement too.
responses.forced: The workers arrive. One repeatedly stops to steady himself. The bank grows higher, but Hori no longer points out the places your plan could improve.
responses.delay: The grain remains in your store. Water leaks past the damaged bank. The saving is real; so is the risk you have passed to the people farming below it.

scenes.title: A gift with a shadow
scenes.speaker: landholder
text: Intef arrives without guards. He carries a small loaf. ‘My mother remembered a year like this,’ he says. ‘I would rather not bury people. I also cannot promise every sack my estate owns.’
He offers 24 grain if hungry families promise future labor until their debt is repaid. There is no fixed end date. He calls this security. Tia calls it a door that locks from the outside.

You could negotiate 16 grain in exchange for publicly recorded recognition, with no claim on household labor. Or require a 12-grain contribution from his surplus and publish the rule. His support matters. So do the lives he wants as collateral.
scenes.asideTitle: Ask Intef what he fears losing
scenes.aside: ‘If I give once, every shortage becomes mine to solve. If I refuse, everyone remembers only my full store.’ You can understand his fear without accepting his terms. Public recognition might motivate a real contribution. Mixed motives do not make every benefit false. The stone offers a question from your old life: would you accept these terms if you woke tomorrow in the body of the person taking the loan?
choices: bargain
Negotiate a fixed contribution and public credit, without labor debt (+16 grain).
debt
Accept the larger loan secured by household labor (+24 grain).
levy
Require a proportionate surplus contribution with a published reason (+12 grain).
refuse
Refuse his help rather than owe him influence.

responses.bargain: Intef wants his name spoken at the reopening. You agree to record the actual contribution, not promise him control. His pride has helped fund something useful. Now you must keep the bargain honest.
responses.debt: The sacks arrive. Tia reads the obligation twice. ‘When do they become free of it?’ she asks. The agreement has no answer. You have solved one shortage by creating another kind of insecurity.
responses.levy: Intef pays and leaves angry. You explain the same proportion will apply to any comparable surplus, including your own. A just demand can still create an opponent.
responses.refuse: Intef takes the loaf home. You have avoided his conditions. You also have fewer ways to meet the village’s needs. Independence is a means, not a meal.

scenes.title: The missing measure
scenes.speaker: scribe
text: At sunset, Djehu discovers a measure missing. Someone names a young worker. A guard is already leading him forward. ‘Make an example,’ a voice says. ‘Otherwise tomorrow everyone will steal.’
Hori says the worker carried a ration to an injured friend. Tia says she saw a basket spill near the door. Djehu’s board contains a corrected mark. None of those facts tells the whole story.

The worker’s hands shake. You could punish him, hide the discrepancy, forgive him immediately, or stop to compare the record with witnesses. Keeping order is part of your duty. So is asking what kind of order you are keeping. Impartiality means judging without unfairly favoring either side—even when one person is powerful or one story is satisfying.
scenes.aside: The original mark counted a delivery twice. That may explain part of the shortage, but it does not prove everything the worker says. A fair inquiry needs both the corrected account and the people who saw the delivery. Evidence can complicate a satisfying story. Independent support for a claim is corroboration. Three people repeating one rumor are still relying on one source.
choices: investigate
Hear witnesses and correct the account before assigning responsibility.
punish
Punish the accused worker to discourage future theft.
conceal
Quietly change the record so the village appears well managed.
mercy
Release the worker without investigating; compassion matters most.

responses.investigate: The doubled entry explains the missing measure. The worker did carry food to his injured friend, with permission nobody recorded. You correct both failures. Djehu looks embarrassed, then relieved: telling the truth did not cost him his place.
responses.punish: The courtyard learns to fear an accusation. Later, the doubled entry comes to light. The grain was never missing. Your certainty has injured someone the evidence could have protected.
responses.conceal: The totals now match. Djehu knows they match because you ordered them to. Tomorrow, a real shortage will be harder to distinguish from a convenient number.
responses.mercy: The worker goes home grateful. The accounting error remains unexplained. Kindness protected him today, but a fair procedure could protect the next accused person too.

scenes.title: What does order require?
scenes.speaker: scribe
text: Djehu stays after the others leave. ‘You keep asking what makes an order fair. We speak of ma’at: truth, justice, and the proper order of the world. But powerful people can say “order” when they mean “leave my place untouched.”’
The stone in your palm warms. A sentence appears like light beneath water: A village can be quiet because it trusts its leaders—or because it fears them.

Djehu asks what principle you want written beside your seal. Your old classroom’s four lenses return: authority, custom, reasons, and consequences. They can work together. They can also expose what another lens hides. These are your modern tools for examining this fictional situation, not a claim that every ancient Egyptian used this framework.
scenes.aside: Authority: who has a recognized right to decide? Custom: what established practice are people relying on? Reasons: what supports a decision, and would the same reasoning apply to a powerful friend? Consequences: who benefits, who suffers, and what happens later? Ma’at joins truth, justice, and proper order in an Egyptian religious world. Dignity calls for respectful treatment. Duty asks what you owe because of your role or relationship. Use these ideas together; the oldest rule or strongest official does not automatically settle the question.
choices: balance
Use my authority to test custom, give fair reasons, and check consequences.
obedience
Authority and custom settle it: people should obey the administrator.
kindness
My generous intentions are enough; consequences cannot make the decision wrong.

responses.balance: Djehu writes slowly. “Then the record must include people an impressive total leaves out.” You have connected authority to reasons that can be challenged, custom to circumstances, and consequences to actual lives. The stone offers no certificate of goodness. It offers a standard you can be asked to meet.
responses.obedience: ‘Then a frightened village and a flourishing one may look identical on your board,’ Djehu says. The stone remains warm. It is waiting for you to notice the difference.
responses.kindness: ‘Generosity matters,’ Djehu says, ‘but seed eaten kindly does not grow.’ Your motive belongs in the story. It does not erase everyone else’s experience of the result.

scenes.title: Tomorrow’s bread
scenes.speaker: household
text: Tia returns with a child asleep against her shoulder. You can see now how easily the word “household” hides a person. She does not ask for a speech about the future. She asks whether there will be bread tomorrow.

There are 20 measures of seed grain set aside. Eating seed can relieve an emergency. It also means planting less. Hori says the repaired bank—if you funded it—makes protecting seed especially valuable. If the bank remains weak, seed alone is no guarantee.

You can protect all the seed, release five measures as a limited emergency ration, or use fifteen. None of these choices creates new grain. Your earlier decisions determine how desperate this moment has become. Your role gives you a duty to respond. It does not give you the ability to guarantee everything.
scenes.asideTitle: Ask what Tia would count as a promise
scenes.aside: ‘Do not promise that no one will ever be hungry. Promise to tell us what remains, who receives it, and when you will reconsider. A promise I can question is worth more than a beautiful promise I cannot check.’ Dignity is the worth that calls for respectful treatment. It does not depend on whether the person asking is convenient, grateful, or powerful.
choices: preserve
Protect all seed and explain the remaining food ration.
ration
Release five seed measures for urgent needs; protect the other fifteen.
consume
Release fifteen seed measures to relieve more hunger now.

responses.preserve: The seed stays sealed. The future has a better chance. Tia asks you to remember the people who still have to reach it.
responses.ration: Five measures leave the seed store under a recorded emergency rule. It is a compromise, not a miracle: less hunger now, less planting later.
responses.consume: Children eat. Tia thanks you. Hori looks at the nearly empty seed store and asks what the lower fields will grow. Both responses are true.

scenes.title: The administrator is a person too
scenes.speaker: worker
text: You wake before dawn with a headache. Every dispute now arrives at your door. A leaking jar. A missing tool. A cousin who wants a larger share. You remember a different life, school corridors, the bus, a person you hope survived.

Hori finds you asleep over the accounts. ‘If you must approve every repair, the canal will wait whenever you close your eyes.’ Djehu proposes a small team with clear responsibilities and an open record. Intef offers to take all the decisions off your hands.
Rest can look selfish when others are struggling. But exhaustion can also turn your generosity into a system nobody else can operate.
scenes.aside: ‘Give us authority to fix small problems and a rule for reporting what we use. Let Tia check who receives food. Let Djehu keep the account. Then someone can catch my mistakes as well as yours.’ Trust needs both room to act and ways to answer for actions.
choices: delegate
Share defined responsibilities and rest, while keeping decisions open to review.
alone
Keep every decision yourself and work through the night.
elite
Hand control to Intef; he has experience and resources.

responses.delegate: For the first time, a problem is solved without waking you. Delegating has not made you unnecessary. It has made the village less dependent on your endurance.
responses.alone: You settle three disputes and misread a fourth. People praise your dedication. Your body is asking whether praise can replace sleep.
responses.elite: The queue at your door disappears. It reforms outside Intef’s house. Your relief is real, but the village has fewer people it can question.

scenes.title: Whose name remains?
scenes.speaker: landholder
text: Intef points to the granary wall. ‘You could put your name there. People remember a name longer than a ration.’ You feel the attraction. In this borrowed life, perhaps you could leave proof you mattered.

Tia wants the account displayed: what came in, what went out, and who can challenge it. Hori wants the workers named. Djehu says there is room for a record of contributions, but a grand monument will cost eight measures of grain.

Wanting to be remembered is not automatically corrupt. A useful legacy can begin in pride. The question is what your desire for recognition asks other people to pay. Accountability means being answerable for what you do. An impressive name on a wall can invite questions—or distract from them.
scenes.aside: If you negotiated grain for public credit, honest acknowledgment keeps your promise. Credit need not mean unlimited praise or authority. If you required a contribution, record it accurately too. Public truth should not depend on whether you like the contributor.
choices: publish
Display the accounts, promises, and all actual contributions—including yours.
monument
Spend eight grain on a monument celebrating your leadership.
credit
Honor the workers and contributors, with a modest record of your own role.

responses.publish: Your name appears among others. So do the costs and the remaining problems. Anyone can see what you achieved—and what you did not. This is a riskier kind of remembrance than a flattering inscription.
responses.monument: The stonecutter promises an impressive inscription. Eight measures leave the store. The village will remember your name. What it associates with that name is less certain.
responses.credit: Hori reads the workers’ names aloud. Intef listens for his contribution. Recognition has become something to share rather than something only the administrator can own.

scenes.title: A village beyond you
scenes.speaker: household
text: The pale line inside your stone is now a complete circle. You know, without being told, that this life is nearly finished. The village does not know. For them, tomorrow is not an epilogue.
Tia lays a hand on the granary door. ‘A good administrator can die. A bad one can inherit the seal. What have we got then?’

You can leave a council that includes households and workers, or train a successor with public records and a way to appeal decisions. Either can fail; either gives the village something beyond your intentions. You could instead trust your reputation, or spend one final generous ration and let tomorrow’s leader worry about tomorrow.
scenes.aside: Tia answers immediately: ‘The person with the least to lose can always speak. I want the person with the most to lose to be able to speak too.’ A council needs more than seats. A successor needs more than your confidence. The agreement must name how complaints are heard and how decisions can be corrected.
choices: council
Leave a representative council, public accounts, and a protected route for complaints.
successor
Train a successor and establish public reviews and appeals.
secrecy
Leave the seal to a loyal ally and keep the accounts private.
empty
Give a final generous ration; leave the next crisis to the next leader (12 grain).

responses.council: Tia and Hori argue about the first rule. Nobody asks you to settle it immediately. You feel a small loss of importance—and the beginning of something that might outlast you.
responses.successor: Djehu repeats the appeal procedure without looking at his board. Your successor will have power. Other people will have a named way to question how it is used.
responses.secrecy: Your ally promises loyalty. You realize too late that loyalty to your name is not the same thing as responsibility to the village.
responses.empty: The last distribution brings warm thanks. The next leader will inherit those grateful faces along with a thinner store. You hope they will find a solution you have not left them.
